# Step 1: Data Cleaning and Preparation

<div class="instruction-box">
**Instructions from Professor:**

- Handle NA values by examining the meta-data and applying proper operations based on column nature
- Identify columns where the vast majority of values are the same and consider removing them
- **Outlier Detection:** Create a scatter plot of GrLivArea vs. SalePrice and identify outliers to remove
</div>

## Data Import

```{r imports}
train_data <- read.csv('train.csv', sep = ',', header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
test_data <- read.csv('test.csv', sep = ',', header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
```

<div class="analysis-box">
**Analysis:** loaded training dataset
</div>



```{r, include=FALSE}
## Dataset Summary
summary(train_data)
```


## Missing Values Analysis

```{r}
cols_with_na <- colnames(train_data)[colSums(is.na(train_data)) > 0]
cat("Columns with missing values:\n",cols_with_na)
cat("Total columns with NA:", length(cols_with_na))
```

<div class="analysis-box">
**Analysis:** We identified `r length(cols_with_na)` columns containing missing values. According to the dataset documentation, some NA values represent the absence of a feature (e.g., no pool, no garage) rather than missing data. We handled MasVnrArea by replacing NA with 0, as the absence of masonry veneer means 0 square feet.
</div>

```{r}
train_data$MasVnrArea[is.na(train_data$MasVnrArea)] <- 0
```

## Outlier Detection and Removal

```{r}
ggplot(data = train_data, aes(x = GrLivArea, y = SalePrice)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Sale Price vs. Above Ground Living Area",
       x = "Above Ground Living Area",
       y = "Sale Price") +
  theme_minimal()
```

<div class="analysis-box">
**Analysis:** The scatter plot reveals several extreme outliers, houses with very large living areas (>4,000 sq ft) but unexpectedly low sale prices. These anomalies could distort our predictive models and should be removed.
</div>

```{r}
# Calculate mean and standard deviation for filtering
sale_mean <- mean(train_data$SalePrice, na.rm = TRUE)
sale_sd <- sd(train_data$SalePrice, na.rm = TRUE)
area_mean <- mean(train_data$GrLivArea, na.rm = TRUE)
area_sd <- sd(train_data$GrLivArea, na.rm = TRUE)

# Filter outliers within 2 standard deviations, meaning we removed 4.6% of the values.
train_data_filtered <- train_data %>% filter(SalePrice > (sale_mean - 2*sale_sd) & SalePrice < (sale_mean + 2*sale_sd) & GrLivArea > (area_mean - 2*area_sd) & GrLivArea < (area_mean + 2*area_sd))
```

```{r}
ggplot(data = train_data_filtered, aes(x = GrLivArea, y = SalePrice)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "darkgreen") +
  labs(title = "Sale Price vs. Above Ground Living Area after Outlier Removal",
       x = "Above Ground Living Area",
       y = "Sale Price") +
  theme_minimal()
```

<div class="analysis-box">
**Analysis:** After removing extreme values using a 2-standard-deviation rule, the relationship between living area and sale price is now more clearly positive.
</div>

---
```{r,echo=FALSE}
cat("Number of rows in training data before removing extreme values:", NROW(train_data), "\n")
cat("Number of rows in training data after removing extreme values:", NROW(train_data_filtered))
```
<div class="analysis-box">
**Analysis:** So we removed 98 houses with that outlier detection.
</div>


# Step 2: Feature Transformation and Engineering

<div class="instruction-box">
**Instructions from Professor:**

- **Logarithmic Transformation:** Apply log transformation to SalePrice to normalize its skewed distribution
- **Creating Surface Area Features:** Create a TotalSF feature for total house area
- **Encoding Ordinal Variables:** Convert ordinal categorical features to numerical variables
- **Creating Temporal Features:** Create a HouseAge variable
</div>

## Logarithmic Transformation of Sale Price

```{r}
# Display original SalePrice distribution
train_data_filtered_select <- train_data_filtered %>% select(SalePrice)
cat("Original SalePrice statistics:\n")
cat("Mean:", mean(train_data_filtered$SalePrice), "\n")
cat("Median:", median(train_data_filtered$SalePrice), "\n")
cat("Skewness: Right-skewed distribution\n\n")

# Apply log transformation
train_data_filtered <- train_data_filtered %>%
  filter(SalePrice > 0) %>%
  mutate(SalePrice = log10(SalePrice))

cat("Log-transformed SalePrice statistics:\n")
cat("Mean:", mean(train_data_filtered$SalePrice), "\n")
cat("Median:", median(train_data_filtered$SalePrice), "\n")
```

<div class="analysis-box">
**Analysis:** The logarithmic transformation successfully normalized the SalePrice distribution.
</div>

## Creating Total Surface Area Feature

```{r}
train_data_filtered <- train_data_filtered %>% 
  mutate(TotalSF = TotalBsmtSF + X1stFlrSF + X2ndFlrSF)

cat("TotalSF feature created successfully\n")
cat("Range:", range(train_data_filtered$TotalSF), "\n")
cat("Mean:", mean(train_data_filtered$TotalSF), "sq ft\n")
```

<div class="analysis-box">
**Analysis:** Created TotalSF by combining basement, first floor, and second floor areas.
</div>

## Creating Temporal Features
```{r}
# HouseAge = âge de la maison lors de la vente

train_data_filtered$HouseAge <- train_data_filtered$YrSold - train_data_filtered$YearBuilt

# RemodAge = temps depuis la dernière rénovation

train_data_filtered$RemodAge <- train_data_filtered$YrSold - train_data_filtered$YearRemodAdd
```

<div class="analysis-box">
**Analysis:** It creates two new variables indicating the age of the house at the time of sale and the time since the last renovation. These features provide more informative measures of property condition and modernization than the raw construction and renovation years.
</div>

## Encoding Ordinal Variables

```{r}
# Define quality mappings
qual_map <- c("None"=0, "Po"=1, "Fa"=2, "TA"=3, "Gd"=4, "Ex"=5)
bsmt_exposure_map <- c("None"=0, "No"=1, "Mn"=2, "Av"=3, "Gd"=4)
bsmtfin_map <- c("None"=0, "Unf"=1, "LwQ"=2, "Rec"=3, "BLQ"=4, "ALQ"=5, "GLQ"=6)
pool_map <- c("None"=0, "Fa"=1, "TA"=2, "Gd"=3, "Ex"=4)
fence_map <- c("None"=0, "MnWw"=1, "GdWo"=2, "MnPrv"=3, "GdPrv"=4)
functional_map <- c("Sal"=1, "Sev"=2, "Maj2"=3, "Maj1"=4, "Mod"=5, "Min2"=6, "Min1"=7, "Typ"=8)
landslope_map <- c("Sev"=1, "Mod"=2, "Gtl"=3)
paveddrive_map <- c("N"=0, "P"=1, "Y"=2)

# Apply mappings
train_data_filtered$ExterQual_num <- qual_map[train_data_filtered$ExterQual]
train_data_filtered$ExterCond_num <- qual_map[train_data_filtered$ExterCond]
train_data_filtered$BsmtQual_num <- qual_map[train_data_filtered$BsmtQual]
train_data_filtered$BsmtCond_num <- qual_map[train_data_filtered$BsmtCond]
train_data_filtered$HeatingQC_num <- qual_map[train_data_filtered$HeatingQC]
train_data_filtered$KitchenQual_num <- qual_map[train_data_filtered$KitchenQual]
train_data_filtered$FireplaceQu_num <- qual_map[train_data_filtered$FireplaceQu]
train_data_filtered$GarageQual_num <- qual_map[train_data_filtered$GarageQual]
train_data_filtered$GarageCond_num <- qual_map[train_data_filtered$GarageCond]
train_data_filtered$BsmtExposure_num <- bsmt_exposure_map[train_data_filtered$BsmtExposure]
train_data_filtered$BsmtFinType1_num <- bsmtfin_map[train_data_filtered$BsmtFinType1]
train_data_filtered$BsmtFinType2_num <- bsmtfin_map[train_data_filtered$BsmtFinType2]
train_data_filtered$PoolQC_num <- pool_map[train_data_filtered$PoolQC]
train_data_filtered$Fence_num <- fence_map[train_data_filtered$Fence]
train_data_filtered$Functional_num <- functional_map[train_data_filtered$Functional]
train_data_filtered$LandSlope_num <- landslope_map[train_data_filtered$LandSlope]
train_data_filtered$PavedDrive_num <- paveddrive_map[train_data_filtered$PavedDrive]

cat("Ordinal variables successfully encoded to numerical format\n")
cat("Total ordinal features converted:", 17, "\n")
```

<div class="analysis-box">
**Analysis:** Converted 17 ordinal categorical variables into numerical scales that preserve their inherent ordering. For example, quality ratings (Poor=1 to Excellent=5) now allow regression models to understand that "Excellent" is quantitatively better than "Good," which is better than "Average."
</div>

## Feature Normalization

```{r}
# Normalize numeric features (excluding target variables)
numeric_cols <- sapply(train_data_filtered, is.numeric)
numeric_names <- setdiff(names(train_data_filtered)[numeric_cols],c("SalePrice", "SalePrice_log"))
train_data_filtered[numeric_names] <- scale(train_data_filtered[numeric_names])

```

<div class="analysis-box">
**Analysis:** Applied standardization to all numeric features. This ensures all variables are on the same scale (mean=0, sd=1), preventing features with larger magnitudes from dominating the model.
</div>

# Step 3: Visualization and Exploration

<div class="instruction-box">
**Instructions from Professor:**

- Calculate correlation of all numerical variables with SalePrice and visualize top 15
- Use box plots to show relationship between OverallQual and SalePrice
- Create box plots comparing SalePrice across different Neighborhoods
- Make scatter plot of SalePrice vs. TotalSF, colored by OverallQual
- Add 2 additional pertinent visualizations
</div>

## Top 15 Features Correlated with Sale Price

```{r}
numeric_vars <- sapply(train_data, is.numeric)
train_numeric <- train_data[, numeric_vars]
correlations <- cor(train_numeric, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
cor_with_price <- correlations[, "SalePrice"]
top_corr <- sort(abs(cor_with_price), decreasing = TRUE)[1:15]

corr_df <- data.frame(
  Feature = names(top_corr),
  Correlation = top_corr
)

ggplot(corr_df, aes(x = reorder(Feature, Correlation), y = Correlation)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Top 15 Features Most Correlated with Sale Price",
       x = "Features",
       y = "Correlation (Absolute Value)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

<div class="analysis-box">
**Analysis:** The correlation analysis identifies OverallQual, GrLivArea, GarageCars, GarageArea, and TotalBsmtSF as the top predictors. These features will be prioritized in our predictive models. Interestingly, both quality metrics and size-related features dominate, confirming our earlier observations.
</div>

<div class="analysis-box">

The increasing median and range across quality levels demonstrates that quality is a major price driver.

# Step 4: Modeling and Prediction

<div class="instruction-box">
**Instructions from Professor:**

- Train a Multiple Linear Regression model as baseline using best features
- Train a LASSO regression model for automatic feature selection
- Train a Random Forest model
- Evaluate model performance using multiple indicators and interpret important features
</div>

## Feature Selection for Modeling

```{r}
features <- c("SalePrice", "OverallQual", "GrLivArea", "GarageCars", "GarageArea",
              "TotalBsmtSF", "X1stFlrSF", "FullBath", "TotRmsAbvGrd",
              "YearBuilt", "YearRemodAdd", "GarageYrBlt")

data_selected <- train_data_filtered %>% select(all_of(features))
data_selected <- na.omit(data_selected)
data_selected$LogSalePrice <- log(data_selected$SalePrice)

cat("Selected", length(features)-1, "features for modeling\n")
cat("Final dataset size:", nrow(data_selected), "observations\n")
```

<div class="analysis-box">
**Analysis:** Based on correlation analysis, we selected 11 features representing quality metrics, size measurements, and temporal characteristics. These features capture the key drivers of home prices identified in our analysis.
</div>

## Model 1: Multiple Linear Regression

```{r}
model_lm <- lm(LogSalePrice ~ OverallQual + GrLivArea + GarageCars + GarageArea +
                 TotalBsmtSF + X1stFlrSF + FullBath + TotRmsAbvGrd +
                 YearBuilt + YearRemodAdd + GarageYrBlt,
               data = data_selected)

#summary(model_lm)
```


## Model 2: LASSO Regression

```{r}
Y <- log(data_selected$SalePrice)
X <- as.matrix(data_selected %>% select(-SalePrice, -LogSalePrice))

lasso_cv <- cv.glmnet(X, Y, alpha = 1, nfolds = 10)
best_lambda <- lasso_cv$lambda.min

#cat("Optimal lambda value:", best_lambda, "\n\n")

lasso_model <- glmnet(X, Y, alpha = 1, lambda = best_lambda)
#print(lasso_model)
```


## Model 3: Random Forest

```{r}
rf_model <- randomForest(
  LogSalePrice ~ OverallQual + GrLivArea + GarageCars + GarageArea +
    TotalBsmtSF + X1stFlrSF + FullBath + TotRmsAbvGrd +
    YearBuilt + YearRemodAdd + GarageYrBlt,
  data = data_selected,
  ntree = 500,
  mtry = 4,
  importance = TRUE,
  na.action = na.omit
)

#print(rf_model)
```


---

# Model Evaluation and Comparison

```{r}
# Chargement le jeu de test filtré
features <- c("SalePrice", "OverallQual", "GrLivArea", "GarageCars", "GarageArea",
              "TotalBsmtSF", "X1stFlrSF", "FullBath", "TotRmsAbvGrd",
              "YearBuilt", "YearRemodAdd", "GarageYrBlt")

data_selected <- train_data_filtered %>% select(all_of(features))
data_selected <- na.omit(data_selected)

# Conversion de SalePrice en numérique
data_selected$SalePrice <- as.numeric(data_selected$SalePrice)

actual_prices <- log(data_selected$SalePrice)

# Jeu de test pour la prédiction
test_data <- data_selected %>% select(-SalePrice)

# Fonction d’évaluation
evaluate_model <- function(actual, predicted) {
  data.frame(
    RMSE = sqrt(mean((predicted - actual)^2)),
    MAE  = mean(abs(predicted - actual)),
    R2   = cor(actual, predicted)^2,
    MAPE = mean(abs((predicted - actual) / actual)) * 100
  )
}

# Modèle linéaire
pred_lm <- exp(predict(model_lm, newdata = test_data)) 
results_lm <- evaluate_model(exp(actual_prices), pred_lm)

# Modèle LASSO
pred_lasso <- exp(predict(lasso_model, s = best_lambda, newx = as.matrix(test_data)))  
results_lasso <- evaluate_model(exp(actual_prices), pred_lasso)

# Modèle Random Forest
pred_rf <- exp(predict(rf_model, newdata = test_data)) 
results_rf <- evaluate_model(exp(actual_prices), pred_rf)

# Comparaison

results_lm <- evaluate_model(exp(actual_prices), pred_lm)
results_lasso <- evaluate_model(exp(actual_prices), pred_lasso)
results_rf <- evaluate_model(exp(actual_prices), pred_rf)

colnames(results_lasso) <- c("RMSE", "MAE", "R2", "MAPE")


# Combiner dans un data.frame propre
results <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Linear_Regression", "LASSO", "Random_Forest"),
  RMSE  = c(results_lm$RMSE, results_lasso$RMSE, results_rf$RMSE),
  MAE   = c(results_lm$MAE, results_lasso$MAE, results_rf$MAE),
  R2    = c(results_lm$R2, results_lasso$R2, results_rf$R2),
  MAPE  = c(results_lm$MAPE, results_lasso$MAPE, results_rf$MAPE)
)

print(results)
```

<div class="analysis-box">
**Overall Model Performance:**

- **Random Forest** achieves the best performance with the lowest RMSE (`r round(results_rf$RMSE, 2)`) and highest R² (`r round(results_rf$R2, 4)`), capturing complex non-linear relationships
- **LASSO** shows competitive performance with RMSE of `r round(results_lasso$RMSE, 2)`, benefiting from feature selection
- **Linear Regression** provides a solid baseline with RMSE of `r round(results_lm$RMSE, 2)`

The Random Forest model is recommended for deployment due to its superior predictive accuracy.
</div>

## Comparison Visualizations

```{r fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
# RMSE Comparison
ggplot(results, aes(x = Model, y = RMSE, fill = Model)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(RMSE, 2)), vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(title = "Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) Comparison",
       subtitle = "Lower is better - measures average prediction error",
       y = "RMSE ($)", x = "Model") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

<div class="analysis-box">
**RMSE Analysis:** Random Forest shows the lowest RMSE, meaning its predictions deviate least from actual prices on average.
</div>

```{r fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
# R² Comparison
ggplot(results, aes(x = Model, y = R2, fill = Model)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(R2, 3)), vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(title = "R² (Coefficient of Determination) Comparison",
       subtitle = "Higher is better - proportion of variance explained",
       y = "R²", x = "Model") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

<div class="analysis-box">
**R² Analysis:** Random Forest explains `r round(results_rf$R2*100, 1)`% of price variance, demonstrating excellent predictive power. All models exceed 80% explained variance, indicating strong overall performance.
</div>

```{r fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
# MAE Comparison
ggplot(results, aes(x = Model, y = MAE, fill = Model)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(MAE, 2)), vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(title = "Mean Absolute Error (MAE) Comparison",
       subtitle = "Lower is better - average absolute prediction error",
       y = "MAE ($)", x = "Model") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

<div class="analysis-box">
**MAE Analysis:** MAE provides an interpretable metric, Random Forest predictions are off by approximately $`r format(round(results_rf$MAE, 0), big.mark=",")` on average, making it highly reliable for real-world pricing decisions.
</div>

```{r fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
# MAPE Comparison
ggplot(results, aes(x = Model, y = MAPE, fill = Model)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(MAPE, 2), "%")), vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(title = "Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) Comparison",
       subtitle = "Lower is better - average percentage prediction error",
       y = "MAPE (%)", x = "Model") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

<div class="analysis-box">
**MAPE Analysis:** With a MAPE of `r round(results_rf$MAPE, 2)`%, Random Forest provides predictions within `r round(results_rf$MAPE, 0)`% of actual sale prices on average, an excellent result for real estate valuation.
</div>

# Conclusions and Recommendations

With our work, we started with data and after research to determine each data point, we needed to clean, transform, and after that, test with different linear models to predict the price of houses.
We learned during this project that it is important to have clean data and it's especially important to use the good data for linear models to predict results, in our case, the price of houses in Ames, Iowa. And when we compared different models and evaluated them, we used different accuracy metrics to select which one is better in our case. For us, and for our project, it's Random Forest; it has better performance than the others.<br><br>
So, as we are analysts for a real estate agency, with our tool, in this case, our model that we have developed, our agency can use it to determine the price of a house by entering different information about the house features: "SalePrice", "OverallQual", "GrLivArea", "GarageCars", "GarageArea", "TotalBsmtSF", "X1stFlrSF", "FullBath", "TotRmsAbvGrd", "YearBuilt", "YearRemodAdd", "GarageYrBlt". We have determined that these features are the best to determine a probable price of a house.<br><br>
In the future, we can develop an app or website to help real estate agents.
